title: Inference architecture tuning: Llama/Mistral/Qwen + MoE routing costs (deep dive)
summary: SE-led deep dive on model-specific inference tuning across Llama, Mistral, Qwen and MoE variants. Covered RoPE scaling, KV cache patterns, batching, quantization tradeoffs, and MoE routing overheads for on-prem/VPC deployments. Agreed to run targeted benchmarks (A100/H100) and share kernel/quant results.
topics: KV cache shape & memory impact (multi-query vs multi-head)
Batching strategies and latency SLOs vs throughput
Quantization options: NF4/GPTQ/AWQ and perf tradeoffs
MoE routing: gating cost, expert sharding, and cross-node comms
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-07-21 16:00 PDT (62 mins)
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Joanna Liu (Redwood SE), Dr. Mei Chen (Cobalt ML Platform), Carlos Rivera (Cobalt Staff Eng), Priya Shah (Cobalt Sec)
---
00:00 Samir: Alright everybody, thanks for joining. Quick agenda — Joanna will run through perf notes and then we'll do Q&A, ok?
00:12 Joanna: Great, I'll kick off. Super high level first — we've been seeing three levers drive token cost: kernel selection, KV cache behavior, and batching. With model architecture differences those levers shift a bit.
00:28 Dr. Mei: Quick note — our production tail latency target is 120 ms p95 for chat flows, and peak throughput needs are around 400 reqs/sec for 2k token average. We're mostly on-prem (NVLink clusters) but also want VPC bursting.
00:45 Joanna: Good. So first — RoPE scaling. Llama-style rotary embeddings assume consistent rope freq; when you scale sequence length or do position extrapolation you can hit numeric instability. We recommend the RoPE scaling trick (scale factor tuning) for longer contexts. In practice we tune the scaling multiplier per model; for Llama 2 derivatives a 0.9-0.95 multiplicative factor often reduces hallucination during extrapolation.
01:12 Carlos (interrupt): Sorry, that 0.9 sounds arbitrary — are we seeing perf regressions?
01:18 Joanna: Not perf per se, more quality vs context. But note: RoPE implementations vary — Mistral's attention kernel and Qwen's multi-query layout change the memory pattern for KV cache. So the same RoPE scaling parameter has slightly different impacts on inference speed.
01:35 Samir: Side note, transcription: sometimes our exports show "rope" lowercase or mis-typed as "rope scaling" — ignore that.
01:42 Joanna: Right. On KV cache — Qwen uses multi-query or grouped-kv in some versions which significantly reduces KV memory per layer because keys are shared; that helps throughput on GPU with limited memory but complicates prefix caching since you can't reuse per-head caches the same way.
02:05 Dr. Mei: So Qwen would reduce our GPU memory pressure — is the tradeoff latency or quality?
02:12 Joanna: Mostly memory; if you have heavy parallelism (multi-stream batching) the reduced KV size can let you fit larger batch sizes and reduce p95. But multi-query can increase compute on each token if kernels aren't fused well.
02:28 Joanna: For MoE — the big items are: routing cost (the gating network), extra all-to-all to dispatch tokens to experts across devices, and memory for expert activations. For on-prem NVLink clusters you can mitigate cross-node bandwidth if you carefully co-locate experts and route by affinity. But there's an irreducible CPU/GPU overhead for routing per token.
02:50 Carlos: Can we quantify that? Rough numbers?
02:53 Joanna: Very rough: gating + routing can add 10-30% token latency depending on expert count and shard topology. Cost per token in a throughput sense also increases because effective FLOPs per token rise — though parameter count may be similar, activations multiply.
03:10 Priya: From security perspective, does MoE change audit/logging or encryption needs?
03:16 Samir: Not directly, but it changes your memory and communication patterns — if you're doing KMS-wrapped model loading or HSM-backed key use during inference cold start, the timing and observable telemetry differ. Priya: noted.
03:28 Joanna: On batching — Redwood's runtime continuous batching helps but we recommend adaptive micro-batching: keep batch windows tight for p95, and auto-increase when tails quiet down. For MoE specifically, batching can inadvertently increase routing fanout, so you need a grouping policy that collapses similar tokens or user sessions.
03:48 Dr. Mei: What about quantization? We've tested 8-bit, but want to go down to 4-bit. Which techniques do you recommend?
03:55 Joanna: For 4-bit, our lab prefers NF4/GPTQ variants with per-channel scales; AWQ and SmoothQuant are interesting for activations. The tradeoff is: GPTQ-style methods give better quality retention but sometimes slower kernels unless vendor-optimized. For H100, specialized 4-bit kernels can be much faster, but on older cards (A100) you'll see less lift. We should run the same quant run across A100/H100 and compare latency and perplexity drop.
04:25 Carlos: Any specific kernels we should try?
04:28 Joanna: Try cuBLAS+FlashAttention fused kernels, vendor-supplied Q4 kernels, and Redwood's quant-aware execution path that picks grouped matmul kernels. We'll share a benchmark spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/bench/cobalt-2025)
04:44 Samir: Note — the link is a placeholder; we'll upload the real perms.
04:50 Joanna: On rope scaling and MoE together — one gotcha is that gating can be sensitive to position encoding differences; if your gating network trained with a different positional scheme you may see alternative expert selection distributions at long contexts. So test gating stability during extrapolation.
05:12 Dr. Mei: How about shard topology? We have 8xA100s per node with NVLink. Best practice?
05:19 Joanna: If you can keep experts intra-node via NVLink, you avoid inter-node all-to-all for expert dispatch. That reduces latency and network egress. If you must span nodes, group experts per NVLink domain and use asynchronous dispatch for low-priority batches.
05:37 Carlos: Does Redwood support colocated expert placement in Dedicated / Private?
05:40 Samir: Yes, our Private offering gives placement hints and node-affinity controls. Joanna: we also have automatic expert-shard planner that tries to minimize cross-node comms. It's not perfect — you still need to tune expert counts and gating temperature.
05:55 Joanna: On gating temperature — increasing temperature softens the gate and increases token fanout (more experts activated), which hurts throughput. Lower temperature makes gates sharper but can lose model capacity. Typical tuning pattern: sweep temp from 0.5 -> 1.2 and measure both quality and tokens-per-expert to find efficient operating point.
06:18 Priya: Any PCIe vs NVLink considerations for VPC bursting?
06:22 Joanna: Yes — cloud burst nodes often attach via PCIe interconnects; NVLink intra-node traffic is much cheaper and faster. For VPC bursts, prefer models/rollouts that can tolerate slightly higher p95 or use a fallback model that's cheaper. Also consider reduced-context fallback to keep latency bounded.
06:40 Carlos: What about prefix/KV cache strategies for chat history? We push 3-4 turns to model.
06:45 Joanna: Use prefix KV caching on a per-session basis; don't cache across users. For long-running sessions consider selective caching (cache only the last N tokens or important utterances). Also, for Qwen-like multi-query models cache sizes are smaller but you need to adjust your eviction policy because you lose per-head granularity. We recommend per-session TTL of 30 mins and an LRU for memory-bounded caches.
07:10 Dr. Mei: Will Redwood's runtime auto-evict?
07:13 Samir: We provide cache eviction hooks and policies you can tune via the console. We'll send recommended defaults.
07:20 Joanna: A few more gotchas: 1) Attention fusion — some model variants (Mistral derivatives) benefit a lot from GQA/fused kernels; if you're running a generic kernel you may be slower by 20-40%. 2) RoPE implementation differences can cause tiny per-token compute diffs if not vectorized.
07:40 Carlos: Ok can we tie this to a concrete bench plan?
07:44 Joanna: Proposed bench: baseline (fp16) Llama-like model, then Mistral variant, Qwen variant, and MoE variant. For each: run A100 and H100, measure p50/p95 p99 latency for 1-2k token scenarios, tokens/sec throughput at 8k/16k contexts, and quality metrics (ROUGE/perp on 200 prompts). Also test NF4/GPTQ/AWQ quantized paths and record memory, latency delta, and quality delta. We'll run with and without KV cache warming.
08:15 Dr. Mei: That sounds good. Timeline?
08:18 Samir: We can spin up the jobs next week if you give us access to a test cluster (or we can run on Redwood Dedicated infra and share traces).
08:26 Priya: Security — we'll need an NDA addendum and SOC-2 attestation before you run on our infra. Also, KMS integration for any model artifacts.
08:35 Samir: Noted; we'll share security pack.
08:38 Joanna: Questions?
08:41 Carlos: In MoE, does expert offloading to CPU ever make sense?
08:44 Joanna: Offloading helps when you run out of GPU memory for expert activations and when latency isn't super tight. But offloading raises tail latency unpredictably and is generally a last resort for cost-limited workloads.
08:58 Dr. Mei: Any recommended guardrails to keep costs down with MoE?
09:02 Joanna: Limit expert fanout via gating temp, reduce expert count, and use smaller expert hidden dims. Also consider a hybrid model: base dense for short contexts and MoE for long-running jobs.
09:15 Carlos: For the quant kernels, do you recommend open-source runtime or vendor libs?
09:19 Joanna: Use vendor libs where possible for production (H100 optimized), open-source runtimes are fine for exploration. We'll share a matrix.
09:28 Samir: Wrapping up — we'll follow up with a bench plan and security docs, plus a Google sheet for scheduling.
---
